title: Judicial Renaissance -- Ch. 10: Beyond Excellence
keywords: The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary
La Bugal-B'laan Tribal Association v. Ramos
New Code of Judicial Conduct for the Philippine Judiciary
a change of men, but a change in men
primary_topics: Chapter 10 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- a keynote address to a conference of judicial awardees, convened by the SC Committee on Judicial Excellence that CJP chairs, to shift the judiciary's public story from the errant to the exalted.

Excellence defined as mastery of law plus a working knowledge of every other branch of human endeavor, demonstrated through six named cases that required economics, mathematics, canon law, biosciences, psychology and mining expertise.

The argument that excellence is not enough: ethics is indispensable, since legally knowledgeable judges without regard for ethics are dangerous to society, and reform requires not a change of men but a change in men.

A third and final quality, eternity: judges should decide with an eye to the hereafter, because spiritual laws operate with consequences like human and physical laws -- yielding the closing exhortation to live by the 3 Es of Excellence, Ethics and Eternity.
sub_topics: CJP recalls the Centenary Lecture Series four years earlier and Israeli Justice Dorit Beinisch, who at a dinner in her honor congratulated him for reporting in his book 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' the Court's effort to dismiss, suspend or fine many misfits.

Asked whether the Israeli Supreme Court also disciplined errant judges, Beinisch replied that in half a century it had received only one complaint, and the judge resigned as soon as the Chief Justice privately confronted him -- turning CJP's pleasure into embarrassment.

He notes that because hundreds of Philippine magistrates have been sanctioned, some sectors now imagine the judiciary inhabited by the inept and the corrupt, which is why he has repeatedly explained that competent and honest judges far exceed the incompetent and dishonest.

That conversation led him to promise himself to emphasize the positive, an opportunity that came when he was named chairperson of the SC Committee on Judicial Excellence, tasked with the search for outstanding judges and clerks of court.
He insists recognition should not end with the award ceremonies, since the pursuit of excellence should be a conscious and continuing endeavor.

The Conference gathers all judicial awardees since 1991, when the Foundation for Judicial Excellence began the search, until the year the Supreme Court took over, for a threefold purpose: to encourage awardees, to inspire others, and to formulate an action plan for excellence in the whole judiciary.

He reports programs already under way -- awardees invited as guest speakers at APJR-related functions, arranged interviews on radio, TV and print by the SC Public Information Office, and priority in judicial promotion.

He invites further proposals, including recognizing exemplary awardees as national artists are recognized, improving the yearly awards, and a Search Committee of awardees to nominate deserving judges who may feel it beneath their dignity to apply personally.

Excellence, the first quality, demands mastery of one's chosen vocation plus general knowledge of the arts, history, philosophy, mathematics, physics, psychology, medicine, economics, health, computers and the latest biosciences and biotechnologies.

Six cases illustrate why: Tanada v. Angara required grappling with globalization, trade liberalization, privatization and deregulation and with the 36-volume WTO Treaty; Veterans Federation Party v. Comelec required mathematics for the party-list formula.

Santos v. Court of Appeals and Republic v. Molina required Catholic Canon Law to understand psychological incapacity under Article 36 of the Family Code; People v. Vallejo and People v. Yatar required the new biosciences behind DNA testing.

CJP adds that after two bioscience seminars in Hawaii and Canada he realized the bio-age was just dawning, a subject treated in his books 'The Bio-Age Dawns on the Judiciary' and 'Leveling the Playing Field.'

People v. Genosa required recent psychological studies on the battered woman syndrome; La Bugal-B'laan Tribal Association v. Ramos required environmental, financial, technical and social analysis of the 1995 Mining Law.

Ethics is the second quality: awardees must rigorously follow the Canons of Judicial Ethics and the New Code of Judicial Conduct and be epitomes of integrity, courage, fidelity, prudence and selflessness.

He observes that most administrative cases against judges and judicial employees involve ethical violations -- bias, dishonesty, misconduct, immorality, abuse of discretion, undue delay, knowingly rendering unjust judgments, dereliction, negligence and unbecoming conduct.

Reform therefore requires transforming old habits of laziness, ineptness and duplicity into ethical values of industry, competence and honesty; the knowledgeable but unethical judge may be worse than the criminals he sentences.
Eternity is the third quality: ideal judges must act knowing their decisions will be remembered not only in this life but in the next, and will want a place in a zillion tomorrows.

He develops an analogy among civil, criminal, physical and spiritual laws -- each with its consequences for breach -- and notes that just as there is reparation there is salvation through repentance, restitution and reformation.
He ends with the exhortation to remember the 3 Es of a life worth living, to make them guiding lights and supplications, and to radiate them not by empty words but by daily example.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reproduces a fifteen-minute keynote Justice Panganiban delivered to a conference of judicial awardees convened by the Supreme Court Committee on Judicial Excellence, which he chaired. He began with a memory from the Court's centenary four years earlier, when Israeli Justice Dorit Beinisch congratulated him for reporting in his book 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' the Court's effort to dismiss, suspend and fine many misfits; when he asked whether the Israeli Supreme Court also disciplined errant judges, she replied that in half a century it had received only one complaint, and the judge resigned when privately confronted -- a reply that turned his pleasure into embarrassment and led him to resolve to emphasize the positive. Because hundreds of Philippine magistrates had been sanctioned, he said, some sectors had formed the impression that the judiciary was inhabited by the inept and the corrupt, when in truth the competent and honest far exceeded them. The Conference gathered every awardee since the Foundation for Judicial Excellence began the search in 1991, with a threefold purpose: to encourage awardees, to inspire others, and to formulate an action plan for excellence, veering the focus from the errant to the exalted. He then set out the qualities to look for. Excellence demands mastery of law plus a working knowledge of every other field, since judges cannot merely be walking databases of the Constitution, the law and jurisprudence; he illustrated this with six rulings -- Tanada v. Angara, in which he had to read the 36-volume WTO Treaty; Veterans Federation Party v. Comelec and its mathematical formula; Santos and Molina on Canon Law and psychological incapacity; Vallejo and Yatar on DNA; Genosa on the battered woman syndrome; and La Bugal-B'laan on the 1995 Mining Law. Ethics, he argued, is indispensable, since knowledgeable judges without it are dangerous and reform requires not a change of men but a change in men. Finally he urged an eternal perspective, comparing spiritual laws to civil, criminal and physical ones, and closed by exhorting his audience to live the 3 Es -- Excellence, Ethics and Eternity.
